title: Phonon-Mediated Superconductivity near Phase Boundaries in Rhombohedral Multilayer Graphene
abstract: The recent observation of superconductivity in untwisted multilayer graphene has sparked intense interest in its microscopic origin. As the displacement field and carrier density are varied, superconductivity emerges in several distinct regions with different temperature and magnetic-field responses. This behavior has been attributed to the presence of distinct electronic phases, raising the possibility that different superconducting regions originate from different microscopic mechanisms. While purely electronic pairing mechanisms have been extensively explored, an in-depth examination of phonon-mediated superconductivity is still missing. Here, we solve the coupled selfconsistent Migdal-Eliashberg equations using input from first-principles calculations and incorporating interaction-driven symmetry breaking of the electronic ground state. Varying the carrier density and displacement field, we reproduce the experimentally observed superconducting regions with comparable superconducting properties such as gap and $T_c$ and predict additional, as-yet undiscovered superconducting phases. Our findings exemplify that several superconductivity regions in rhombohedral graphene can be satisfactorily explained by phonon-mediated pairing.
summary: This theoretical study explores superconductivity in multilayer graphene by solving the Migdal-Eliashberg equations, focusing on phonon-mediated pairing. The authors show that phonon coupling, derived from DFT calculations, can successfully explain multiple distinct superconducting phases observed experimentally. The work highlights the interplay between electronic structure, layer number, and lattice vibrations in determining superconducting properties.
main_problem: The paper investigates the microscopic origin of superconductivity in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, specifically determining the relative importance of phonon-mediated pairing versus purely electronic mechanisms near phase boundaries.
main_result: The authors successfully reproduce experimentally observed superconducting regions and predict new phases by modeling the pairing mechanism using phonon-mediated coupling within the Migdal-Eliashberg framework.
method: The study solves the coupled, self-consistent Migdal-Eliashberg equations, utilizing first-principles calculations (DFT+DFPT) to derive phonon dispersions and electron-phonon coupling matrix elements.
model_or_system: The system is rhombohedral multilayer graphene (N layers), modeled using a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating electron-electron interactions via the Stoner approximation. The superconductivity is governed by solving the Migdal-Eliashberg equations.
key_observables: Superconducting gap ($\Delta$), critical temperature ($T_c$), and the electronic Density of States (DoS) across different flavor degeneracies ($\gamma$).
important_parameters: Carrier density, displacement field, and the number of graphene layers (N=2 to 6).
main_assumptions: The Stoner approximation is used for symmetry breaking, and the full self-consistent treatment including electron-phonon retardation is noted as a limitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of the DoS with doping/displacement field, the phonon dispersion and electron-phonon coupling strength ($V_{eph}$) vs. layer number, and the calculated superconducting gap ($\Delta$) in various doping regimes for trilayer and tetralayer graphene.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the electronic structure and flavor degeneracy using the Stoner model, then calculating the necessary electron-phonon coupling parameters via DFT+DFPT, and finally solving the Migdal-Eliashberg equations to map out the superconducting phase diagram.
why_interesting: While focused on graphene, the methodology of using advanced many-body theory (Migdal-Eliashberg) combined with first-principles calculations to map out complex phase diagrams is highly relevant to understanding pairing mechanisms in novel quantum materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. DoS calculated as function of electron doping ne and displacement field D for rhombohedral graphene with (a)-(d): N = 2, 3, 4, and 5 layers. Colors denote the flavor degener- acy: full metal (γ = 4, green), half-metal (γ = 2, blue), and quarter-metal (γ = 1, red). The colormap is normalized to the maximum density of states in the electron- and hole-doped region, with ρ(h) max and ρ(e) max given in each panel. Units are in eV−1nm−2. The Stoner parameters are (U, J) = (60, −9), (30, −9), (13, −18) and (11, −14) eV for (a)-(d).

FIG. 2. (a) Interaction-enhanced density of states ρ of rhom- bohedral trilayer graphene as function of electron doping and at displacement D = 32 meV. Colors denote the flavor de- generacy: full metal (γ = 4, green), half-metal (γ = 2, blue) and quarter-metal (γ = 1, red). (b) Superconducting gap ob- tained from the selfconsistent Migdal-Eliashberg equations at the same densities and T = 25 mK.

FIG. 3. (a) First-principles phonon dispersion of rhombo- hedral tetralayer graphene along the high-symmetry path of the Brillouin zone. (b) Enlargement of the phonon dispersion near the Γ point. The color scale indicates the magnitude of the electron-phonon matrix elements gk+q,ν shown in the colorbar. (c) Phonon-branch resolved electron-phonon cou- pling Veph versus the number of graphene layers, for scatter- ing of electrons at the K valley. The bar height gives the total electron-phonon coupling.

FIG. 4. Superconductivity in rhombohedral trilayer graphene. (a) Calculated superconducting gap, colored by flavor degen- eracy: γ = 2 (blue, SC1 and SC3) and γ = 1 (red, SC2); the two inset color scales give ∆in µeV, blue for γ = 2 and red for γ = 1. The red dashed rectangle marks the γ = 1 window cor- responding to SC2. The calculations are done for T = 75 mK. (b) Superconducting gap evaluated along the gray dotted line in panel (a). (c) Temperature dependence of the gap at the maximum of panel (b).

FIG. 5. Predicted superconductivity in rhombohedral tetra- layer graphene. (a) Appearance of various superconducting gaps (SC1 −SC4) in the electron-doped regime. (b) Super- conducting gap in the hole-doped regime with two supercon- ducting regions SC1 and SC2. (c) Maximum superconducting gap as a function of the density of states obtained using the first-principles electron-phonon coupling for different numbers of graphene layers. All calculations are done for T = 25 mK.
